data.title: Persons providing services to a corporation or partnership
data.text:
(1) Subject to subrules (2) and (3), if (a) a party cannot obtain relevant and material information from an officer or employee or a former officer or former employee of a corporation or partnership that is a party adverse in interest, (b) it would be unfair to require the party seeking the information to proceed to trial without having the opportunity to ask questions about the information sought, and (c) the questioning will not cause undue hardship, expense or delay to, or unfairness to, any other party or to the person to be questioned, the party may question, under oath, a person who has provided services for the corporation or partnership and who can provide the best evidence on the issue.
(2) A person described in subrule (1) may be questioned only (a) by written agreement of the parties, or (b) with the Court’s permission.
(3) An expert engaged by a party for the purposes of the action may not be questioned under this rule.

data.title: Limit or cancellation of questioning
data.text:
On application, the court may do either or both of the following:
(a) limit the number of persons subject to questioning by a party;
(b) cancel an appointment for questioning that the court considers unnecessary, improper or vexatious.
[2017] A.J. No. 177,  ABQB 106 at para. 466 (Alta Q.B.); , [2015] A.J. No. 638, Rotzang v. CIBC World Markets Inc. ABQB 106 at para. 462 (Alta. Q.B.).

data.title: When questioning is to take place
data.text:
(1) Unless the parties otherwise agree, or the court in exceptional circumstances otherwise orders, a party may not question a party or person under this Division unless the questioning party has served an affidavit of records on the party adverse in interest.
(2) Subject to subrule (1), the questioning of a person is to take place as follows:
(a) questioning by the plaintiff, at any time after (i) a statement of defence has been served on the plaintiff, or (ii) the time for serving the statement of defence has expired;
(b) questioning by the defendant and every other party, at any time after a statement of defence has been served.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.20 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

data.text:

rules.title: Oral and written questioning limitations
rules.text:
Unless the parties otherwise agree or the Court otherwise orders, (a) if more than one party is entitled to question a person, the questioning must be oral, and (b) a party may not question a person both orally and by written questioning.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.24 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.title: Appropriate questions and objections
rules.text:
(1) During questioning, a person is required to answer only (a) relevant and material questions, and (b) questions in respect of which an objection is not upheld under subrule (2).
(2) A party or a witness being questioned may object to an oral or written question during questioning but only for one or more of the following reasons:
(a) privilege;
(b) the question is not relevant and material;
(c) the question is unreasonable or unnecessary;
(d) any other ground recognized at law.
(3) A corporate representative may object to an oral or written question during questioning on the basis that it would be unduly onerous for the corporate representative to inform himself or herself in the circumstances.
(4) If an objection to a question cannot be resolved the Court must decide its validity.
(5) After the questioning party has finished questioning a person, that person may be questioned by the party for whom the person is or may be a witness to explain, elaborate or provide context for an answer initially given.
(6) Following answers to the explanatory, elaborative or contextual ques- tions, the person may be questioned again about the person’s answers.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.25 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.title: Transcript of oral questioning
rules.text:
(1) Oral questioning under this Part must be recorded word for word by a person qualified to do so (a) by a method that is capable of producing a written transcript, and (b) in a manner agreed on by the parties or directed by the Court.
(2) The questioning party must make necessary arrangements to record the questioning.
(3) Exhibits produced at the questioning must, unless otherwise agreed by the parties or ordered by the Court, (a) be incorporated in or attached to the transcript, or (b) be produced at the trial of the action without a notice to produce.
[2023] A.J. No. 227,  ABKB 284 at paras. 76-77 (Alta. K.B.); , [2024] A.J. No. 916, 2024 ABCA Simpson v. Pawlowski ABKB 120 at para. 20 (Alta. K.B.), citing , Stoney Indian Band v. Alberta

rules.title: Written questions
sentences: (1) Unless the Court otherwise orders or the parties otherwise agree, the following rules apply with respect to written questions and the answers to them:
(a) the written questions must be numbered and succinct
(b) the answers provided to the questions must be given by affidavit and must state the question being answered
(c) the party being questioned must serve the answers to the questions
(2) A party is entitled to ask
(a) one set of follow-up written questions as a result of the answers to the initial written questions, or
(b) follow-up oral questions if agreed by the parties.

(3) If the answers to the written questions or the answers to the follow-up written or follow-up oral questions are unsatisfactory, the questioning party may apply to the Court for an order for either or both of the following:
(a) oral or further oral questioning
(b) further written questions to be answered. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.28 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)

rules.title: Acknowledgment of corporate witness’s evidence
rules.text:
(1) The evidence given by a corporate witness during questioning may not be read in as evidence at trial unless a corporate representative of the corporation, under oath, acknowledges that the evidence forms some of the information of the corpo- ration.
(2) Subject to subrule (3), the corporate representative may refuse to acknowledge some or all of the evidence of the corporate witness and, if so, must state why, but is not entitled to refuse to acknowledge the corporate witness’s information just because the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with it.
(3) If the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with some or all of the evidence of a corporate witness, the corporate representative (a) must acknowledge the evidence as information of the corporation unless it is inadmissible under the laws of evidence, and R. 5.29 [Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.29 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]

(3) If the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with some or all of the evidence of a corporate witness, the corporate representative

(a) must acknowledge the evidence as information of the corporation unless it is inadmissible under the laws of evidence, and R. 5.29 [Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.29 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]

commentary.text:
The use to which the evidence of a corporate witness (other than the corporate representative) may be put is governed by rule 5.29. A party may examine a corporate party’s current or former officers, employees, or, as may be permitted, service providers, but the evidence cannot be read in at trial unless this rule is complied with. The evidence is admissible only where the statements are admitted or adopted by the corporate representative as some of the information of the corporation. CDM Direct Mail v. Centre for Immigration Policy Reform, [2015] A.J. No. 536, 2015 ABCA 168 at paras. 20-21 (Alta. C.A.). See also , [2016] A.J. No. XS Technologies Inc. v. Veritas DGC Land Ltd. 528, 2016 ABCA 165 at para. 22 (Alta. C.A.); , [2012] A.J. Weatherford Canada Partnership v. Addie No. 352, 2012 ABQB 215 at para. 48 (Alta. Q.B.). Rule 5.29 is a codification of extensive common law rulings under the Former Rules. AMEC Americas Ltd. v. Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co., [2015] A.J. No. 648, Acknowledgement of Evidence – Even where a corporate representative disagrees with the evidence of an employee, there must be an acknowledgement that the evidence given forms some of the information of the corporation, unless it is inadmissible under the laws of evidence at trial. XS Technologies Inc. v. Veritas DGC Land Ltd., [2016] A.J. No. 528, 2016 ABCA 165 at para. 22 (Alta. C.A.).
Practically speaking, a corporate officer who has had excerpts from the discovery of employees or former employees of the corporation made available will usually be required to acknowledge that they form part of the information of the corporation. There may be limited circumstances under which a corporate officer can refuse to acknowledge the evidence as information of the corporation. An example might be a situation where the corporate officer feels the employer did not understand the question because of language difficulties. These situations should arise very infrequently.  1400467 Alberta Ltd. v. Adderley, [2014] A.J. No. 1161, 2014 ABQB 635 at para. 29 (Alta. Q.B.). If the corporate representative disbelieves or disagrees with the evidence, he or she must acknowledge it as information of the corporation and may then qualify the acknowledgement with further evidence. CDM Direct Mail v. Centre for Immigration Policy Reform, [2015] A.J. No. 536, 2015 ABCA 168 at para. 22 (Alta. C.A.).
If the corporate representative was never asked to acknowledge the evidence of a witness, then the evidence cannot be read in under rule 5.29.235

rules.title: Undertakings
rules.text:
(1) If, during questioning, a person answering questions (a) does not know the answer to a question but would have known the answer if the person had reasonably prepared for questioning, or if as a corporate representative the person had reasonably informed himself or herself, or (b) has under the person’s control a relevant and material record that is not privileged, the person must undertake to inform himself or herself and provide an answer, or produce the record, within a reasonable time.
(2) After the undertaking has been discharged, the person who gave the undertaking may be questioned on the answer given or record provided.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.30 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
sentences: (1) If, during questioning, a person answering questions

(a) does not know the answer to a question but would have known the answer if the person had reasonably prepared for questioning, or if as a corporate representative the person had reasonably informed himself or herself, or

(b) has under the person’s control a relevant and material record that is not privileged, the person must undertake to inform himself or herself and provide an answer, or produce the record, within a reasonable time.

(2) After the undertaking has been discharged, the person who gave the undertaking may be questioned on the answer given or record provided. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.30 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
info_notes: Undertakings should be answered in a reasonable time, and the witnesses should generally not delay responding until every undertaking can be answered. The questioner is expected to indicate within a reasonable time whether the undertaking is responsive to the question, and whether the questioner intends to question further on the undertaking. Further questioning should proceed when the undertakings are substantially answered, even if some undertakings remain outstanding, and even if questioning is not completed.

rules.text:

commentary.text:
Due to the often sensitive, personal, and potentially confidential nature of the disclosure obligations required by Part 5 of the Rules, rule 5.33 codifies what was once the “implied undertaking” of confidentiality that arises in litigation, which is designed to safeguard against the potential invasion of privacy. Herchak v. Enbridge Pipelines Inc., [2016] A.J. No. 371, 2016 ABQB 217 at para. 20 (Alta. Q.B.); Makis v. Alberta Health Services Simpson , [2020] A.J. No. 510, 2020 ABCA 168 at para. 61 (Alta. C.A.); v. Pawlowski, [2024] A.J. No. 916, 2024 ABCA 254 at para. 10 (Alta. C.A.). The Supreme Court of Canada has confirmed that both documentary and oral information obtained during discovery is not to be used by the other parties except for the purpose of litigation, unless and until the scope of the undertaking is varied by court order or a situation of immediate and serious danger emerges. Juman v. Doucette, [2008] S.C.J. No. 8, 2008 SCC 8 at para. 4 (S.C.C.). Rule 5.33 limits the use of evidence disclosed prior to trial to the litigation in which it was obtained, unless the implied undertaking is varied by court order or the parties otherwise agree. A breach of rule 5.33 has been found to be analogous to breaching a court order. Kelana Holdings Ltd. v. 393510 Alberta Ltd (c.o.b. Turner Bodyworks and Fabrication) . , [2023] A.J. No. 882, 2023 ABKB 486 at para. 84 (Alta. K.B.), citing , Olkowski v. Nano-Green Biorefineries Inc.
The implied undertaking created by this rule does not apply to court orders, filed affidavits, and cross-examinations on affidavits in an application. Klein v. Wolbeck Hall v. Willcox , [2016] A.J. No. 44, 2016 ABQB 28 at para. 8 (Alta. Q.B.); , These are matters of public record (if not sealed) and, as such, may be referred to in another application. In these instances, the courts are more concerned with protecting the principles of transparency in legal proceedings and the openness of the court record rather than the privacy interests between parties to litigation.
